title: Tulane University (2017/4/3-4/28)
paragraphs: This April, I did a clerkship at Tulane University in New Orleans, at the southern tip of America. Looking back now, jazz was always playing on the street corners, and I feel nostalgic for the streets of New Orleans, bustling with tourists.

As for why I chose America for my clerkship, needless to say it was to study English, but first of all it was because I wanted to grow by taking on a clerkship in America, where the skills and knowledge required are said to be high and strict. Having returned to Japan after finishing the clerkship, honestly I feel relieved to have got through a difficult time. Feelings of having done it all and feelings of frustration are mixed in my heart and not yet sorted out, but what I can say is that it was a much more fruitful experience than I had imagined before leaving.

I was allowed to do a clerkship in obstetrics and gynecology for four weeks. For the first two weeks I did mainly outpatient clerkship at UMC New Orleans, a large new public hospital that had just been built in 2014. Because New Orleans is a region with an especially mixed population even within America, there were people of various races, African, Asian and Latino, all different from build to language, and at first I could not get used to it. Many were from the poor, and among them even prisoners came, accompanied by guards. Also, since it is an area where STDs such as HIV are widespread, I was shocked at how many such patients there were.

Because obstetrics and gynecology is one of the compulsory subjects for third-year students, I was allowed to rotate together with many students. In the clerkship at UMC, the students first did the interview and physical examination of outpatients, presented to the resident, and based on that the resident examined the patient and ordered tests. After that, the students joined the discussion between the resident and the attending about treatment policy and so on, and finally told the patient together with the resident. At first I could not do anything satisfactorily compared with the local students, so I asked the students how to give a presentation, what the interview items were, and so on, and was taught. Not only was there the language barrier, but as for knowledge, too, they studied very well and were excellent, so it was very hard to do work at the same level as them. The doctors' stance was that if you can't do it, you don't have to, so I had to appeal for what I could do. My heart nearly broke, but I made up my mind to make as much effort as possible in order to catch up, asked questions actively, and spent days desperately studying even after the clerkship ended. Thanks to that, toward the end of the second week I became able to do a complete interview and physical examination by myself, and sometimes I was entrusted with simple procedures. I felt my progress and was happy. I think it was precisely because of this environment that I was able to work harder than usual. Also, both the doctors and the students helped me if I actively asked, which I was grateful for. In the third and fourth weeks I trained at Tulane Lake Side Hospital, a hospital 20 to 30 minutes by car from the dormitory. There is no public transport, so I had to find friends to give me rides myself. At worst, a taxi. I asked a different student every day and somehow managed to get there. The flow of the clerkship here was first to do rounds on my own patients before 5 a.m., gather information by looking at charts and asking nurses, and prepare to present. Then if necessary I presented at the conference from 6 o'clock. After that there was a lecture by an attending until 9 o'clock. What was interesting was that there was almost no format of merely explaining slides. They were devised in various ways, such as dividing into teams and competing for points in a quiz format (the winner gets treated to juice and so on), and explaining clearly using Google image search. While desperately following when, in response to students' questions, they smoothly pulled up the latest literature on UpToDate and explained, I felt that for them, whose mother tongue is English, reading English papers is nothing at all, and I envied them for being able to access the latest information without any barrier. After the lecture, we split up into our respective posts, such as deliveries and operations, and did the clerkship.

I was always thinking about and looking for whether American medical care is different from Japan's, and as a level I feel it is broadly the same. What is completely different, however, is the health insurance system. In America, apart from insurance called Medicaid, which only the poor and people with disabilities can join, everything is private commercial insurance. It is not a universal health insurance system like Japan's. And depending on the insurance one has, the surgery one can receive and the drugs prescribed differ. In other words, if you have no money you cannot receive the treatment you want. I think the Japanese healthcare system also has many defects, and I am not saying that the American system is inferior, but seeing the real situation overseas, I felt glad to live in Japan, where everyone can receive medical care of a certain standard.

In the clerkship, there were many differences in the clinical setting from Japan, which made every day fresh and enjoyable: true to America, even women with a BMI over 50 gave birth without concern; because almost everyone has a painless delivery, there is no such thing as the mother shouting from pain during delivery as in Japan (when I said that in Japan no anesthesia is given, everyone's eyes went wide); the guidelines for treatment policy are different from Japan's, for example, if criteria are met even HIV patients can have a vaginal delivery.

The doctors and students I met were mostly people-loving in character, and they called the friendly people of the South "Aggressively welcome" people themselves. They held home parties and barbecues, and I made the best memories.

There were many inconveniences, such as not having access rights to charts (having to borrow a student's ID), conversations being so fast that I sometimes could not keep up, and the town being unsafe, but looking back now, those are trivial compared with the size of the experience gained. Rather, I think that I was given opportunities to grow in proportion to the hardship.

Finally, the dispatch itself to Tulane University was once cancelled, and it came true because the doctors of the International Collaboration Office made efforts and somehow arranged to send me for one month. I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 粕谷, who gave me this valuable experience, everyone at the International Exchange Office of the Nagoya University School of Medicine, and all the staff at my host institution.

Following the clerkship at Tulane University in America in April, I was given the opportunity to do a clerkship at the Chinese University of Hong Kong in May. The reason I chose Hong Kong as my clerkship destination was that the period in America turned out shorter than originally planned, and while looking for my next destination among the limited partner schools, I heard that English education is advanced in Hong Kong and it has an environment in which one can study English. Unlike Japan, there are many young people, and I headed there with expectations in my heart about what medical care is like in lively Asia.

Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China, and because it was a British colony in the past, it has developed a unique culture that, although in Asia, has somehow a Western colour. The city's infrastructure is well developed, and the transport network is as developed as in Japan's urban areas. Also, because the whole country puts effort into English education, the younger generation is fluent in English. There were many doctors at the hospital who had come to study from Europe and Asia, and in fact English was used in conferences and operations in the hospital.

I was allowed to rotate through orthopedics for four weeks at the Prince of Wales Hospital, a huge hospital on the grounds of the Chinese University of Hong Kong. In the first and second weeks it was sports orthopedics. I took part in the clerkship together with exchange students from the University of Hong Kong and Canada. Professor Yung, a very famous sports orthopedic surgeon who had worked as a sports doctor for 15 years, saw many professional athletes in his clinic. Patients, except for overseas athletes, could speak only Cantonese, so I could not do interviews, but they let me do simple physical examinations. He also stopped partway to teach the students enthusiastically in English. He gave me a ticket to a weekend soccer game, and I went to watch it together with the student I was rotating with.

In the third week I trained with the hand surgery team. There are not many hospitals in Hong Kong that have hand surgery and it seems valuable, so the doctors flew around to hospitals everywhere to operate. I followed the doctors and was allowed to scrub in on many operations. On rounds, there were also opportunities to look at X-rays of patients' hands and state the findings, and to actually examine them. To be able to state findings, I studied with a book on reading X-rays in the dormitory. The hand surgeons did very careful and detailed examinations compared with other fields of orthopedics, and I was surprised to see that they spent about 30 minutes per person on rounds. There were also several women doctors who got on with their work energetically, but when I talked with them they were very friendly and warm people. In Hong Kong, dual-income households are normal, and they hire babysitters. For that reason, women do not quit work, and many people continue to build their careers. In Hong Kong, women working is a matter of course in society, so I thought that in that respect Hong Kong is far more advanced than Japan.

In the fourth week I was on the trauma team and spent almost the whole day in the operating room. Whichever doctor I watched operating kindly explained in English. There were only cases well worth seeing, such as a patient with complex fractures in five places from a traffic accident and burns from chemicals.

During the clerkship, in whichever department I rotated, there were doctors and students from overseas who looked after me, so I never once felt lonely. Almost every day the students took me out to lunch off campus, and on days off took me out to have fun. Hong Kong also has beautiful mountains, and the view of Hong Kong's townscape while walking along a mountain ridge called the Dragon's Back is an unforgettable memory. Talking with doctors who had come from overseas for training was also very enjoyable. I became friends with doctors from Italy, Thailand, India and Canada, and chatted with them in spare moments during operations and in the clinic. Hearing about the state of medical care in their countries and how they live as doctors, I think, widened the framework of my values. From an overseas viewpoint, I was often told that Japanese are a people who live for their work. That they are bound by a mould of devoting themselves to others and sacrificing their own time as a matter of course. I too had thought that was a virtue, so seeing overseas doctors who seriously said they would earn plenty of money and use it to travel and eat delicious things and enjoy life, I was shocked to no small degree.

Since studying in America was my first choice, honestly I did not have high expectations of studying in Hong Kong in comparison. But having actually gone, I am sincerely satisfied that I was able to gain a wonderful experience different from America. At first I had the preconception that the medical standard in Hong Kong would be behind Japan's, but it was broadly on par with developed countries, and in some fields even more advanced than Japan.

Besides the clerkship itself, the best thing about going to Hong Kong was meeting wonderful people. When I said I was Japanese, everyone was interested, and they looked after me to a degree that made me wonder how they could do so much. In America, unless I got involved actively myself, no one paid me attention, so I felt a tremendous gap. Also, the doctors in Hong Kong were very diligent, and many were devoted not only to clinical work but also to research. Many were people who were bundles of ambition saying "this is only the beginning," and they gave me energy too.

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 粕谷, who gave me such a valuable experience, everyone at the International Exchange Office of the Nagoya University School of Medicine, and all the staff at my host institution. I would also like to take this opportunity to send encouragement and thanks to Dr. 藤川, who is active in cardiac surgery at the Prince of Wales Hospital and looked after me.
